# Technology Stack

## Project Type

Static-first personal website with dynamic capability for interactive playground items. Markdown-driven content, server-side generated at build time, deployed to edge hosting.

## Core Technologies

### Primary Language(s)
- **Language**: TypeScript (strict mode)
- **Runtime**: Node.js 24 LTS
- **Package Manager**: pnpm

### Framework
- **Next.js** (App Router): React framework handling routing, static generation, and API routes. App Router for layouts, loading states, and server components. Most pages are statically generated at build time; the contact form and any future playground backends use API routes as needed. Next.js ships ~60-85KB of baseline JavaScript on every page (React runtime + client router + navigation components) even when the page content is fully static — this is an accepted tradeoff for the DX benefits of a single framework, single dev server, and single deployment.

### Styling
- **Tailwind CSS v4**: Utility-first CSS framework. Handles all styling including responsive design and dark/light mode.
- **shadcn/ui**: Copy-paste component library built on Radix UI primitives + Tailwind. Components are owned source code, not an installed dependency — fully modifiable to match whatever design language is chosen.

### Content Pipeline
- **MDX**: Markdown with optional embedded React components. Content files use `.mdx` extension. Files that don't use React components behave identically to plain markdown. This is low-cost optionality — MDX compilation is slightly slower than plain markdown, editor previews don't render JSX syntax, and JSX errors produce React compilation errors rather than helpful markdown diagnostics. These are small costs for the ability to embed interactive elements in content if needed.
- **Velite**: Build-time content framework. Defines typed schemas for each content type (blog posts, projects, contributions, resources). Validates frontmatter, generates typed JSON collections. Zero runtime cost.
- **Shiki**: Syntax highlighting for code blocks. Build-time highlighted, no client-side JS. Supports VS Code themes.

### Search
- **Pagefind**: Client-side search. Runs entirely in the browser (~5KB WASM loader; index fetched on demand) — no server, no API. Pagefind indexes rendered HTML via crawler mode: CI runs `next build && next start`, Pagefind crawls the local server to generate the search index, and the index is included in the deploy. This is necessary because Vercel's native Next.js build output (`.next/server/app/`) is not a directory of static HTML files that Pagefind can index directly.

### Key Libraries
- **Radix UI**: Accessible, unstyled UI primitives (via shadcn/ui). Handles complex interactions — dialogs, dropdowns, tooltips — with correct ARIA attributes.
- **react-obfuscate**: Bot-protected email display (click-to-reveal obfuscation) for the contact section.
- **next-themes**: Dark/light mode toggle with system preference detection, no flash of incorrect theme.
- **reading-time**: Estimated reading time for blog posts.
- **rehype/remark plugins**: MDX processing pipeline — table of contents generation, footnotes, GitHub Flavored Markdown, heading anchors.

### Application Architecture
Static-first, single Next.js application. The App Router defines the page hierarchy. Content lives in a `content/` directory as MDX files with frontmatter. Velite processes content at build time into typed JSON. React server components render pages. Client components are used only where interactivity is required (theme toggle, search, contact form, playground items).

### Data Storage
- **Content**: MDX files in `content/` directory, processed at build time by Velite. No database, no CMS.
- **Contact form submissions**: Sent via email through an email SaaS (Resend). No server-side storage of form data.
- **Search index**: Generated by Pagefind at build time, served as static assets.

### External Integrations
- **Resend**: Transactional email API for contact form submissions. Free tier covers 100 emails/day — more than sufficient.
- **GitHub**: Source code hosting, CI/CD trigger.
- **RSS/Atom**: Generated at build time as static XML files.

## Playground Architecture

Playground items are self-contained interactive experiments living under `/playground/[item]`. Two isolation levels:

**Default (most items)**: Separate Next.js routes with dynamically imported components. Style isolation uses CSS `@layer` + CSS Modules: the playground container applies `all: initial` (with explicit overrides for `display`, `box-sizing`, and `unicode-bidi`) to reset inherited styles, sets `isolation: isolate` to establish a stacking context, and all playground CSS is authored in a dedicated `@layer playground` that sits below the site's layer in cascade priority. Each item uses CSS Modules for scoped class names to prevent collisions. Shares the Next.js runtime and bundler but is visually independent from the main site's design. Does not inherit the site's dark/light mode. **Constraint**: playground items must not write global CSS rules or unscoped selectors. Enforced by authorship convention; no automated check. Acceptable because all playground items are first-party.

**Full isolation (iframe)**: Items requiring their own browsing context are loaded via iframe pointing to a dedicated route at `/playground/[item]/embed` (must live under `/playground/` to inherit the permissive playground CSP — not under `/api/`). Complete CSS/JS/dependency isolation. Still built and deployed with the main site.

**Decision rule for iframe isolation**: When in doubt, use iframe — the cost is minimal and the isolation is guaranteed. Use same-page rendering with `@layer` + CSS Modules only for items with scoped styles, no viewport-escaping patterns, and no dependency conflicts. Examples of patterns that require iframe isolation (non-exhaustive):
- Conflicting dependencies not compatible with the main app's dependency tree
- `position: fixed` elements (position relative to viewport, not container)
- Full-viewport layout using `100vw`/`100vh` or other viewport units
- Styles on `:root`, `html`, or `body`
- Third-party libraries that inject global styles
- Custom CSP directives beyond the site's playground policy

**Server-side convention**: Playground items at launch are client-side only. Items needing server capabilities use Next.js API routes under `/api/playground/[item]/`. Credentials are stored in Vercel environment variables. Server-side state or database-backed playground items are evaluated per-item as needed — there is no shared playground backend.

## Development Environment

### Build & Development Tools
- **Build System**: Next.js build (backed by Turbopack in dev, Webpack in production). Note: CSS `@layer` ordering and CSS Modules hashing may differ between bundlers — playground style isolation should be verified via Vercel preview deploys before merging, not just in local dev.
- **Package Management**: pnpm (version pinned via `packageManager` field in `package.json` / Corepack)
- **Version Pinning**: `.nvmrc` for Node.js version, `packageManager` in `package.json` for pnpm version. Ensures reproducible builds across machines and CI.
- **Development workflow**: `next dev` with Turbopack fast refresh

### Code Quality Tools
- **Linting**: ESLint with Next.js config
- **Formatting**: Prettier
- **Testing**: Vitest for unit tests, Playwright for end-to-end tests (scoped to interactive flows: contact form, theme toggle, search, playground loading)
- **Content validation**: CI-time link checker (e.g., lychee) run against the built static output and RSS/XML feeds with fragment checking enabled. Policy: internal links are hard errors (block deploy), external links are warnings (periodic audit). Also validates image references. Catches broken internal links, missing images, and orphaned references — the highest-probability failures on a markdown-driven site. Future enhancement: build-time assertions for duplicate slugs and inconsistent tag casing.
- **Contact form smoke test**: Playwright CI test submits the contact form and verifies a 200 response. Catches silent API route failures that would otherwise go unnoticed.
- **Type checking**: TypeScript strict mode, checked in CI

### Version Control & CI
- **VCS**: Git, hosted on GitHub
- **Branching Strategy**: GitHub Flow — feature branches off main, merged via PR
- **CI/CD**: GitHub Actions — lint, type-check, test, build, deploy on push to main

## Deployment

- **Hosting**: Vercel (Hobby tier). Zero-config Next.js deployment — SSG, SSR, API routes, and edge functions all work out of the box. Free tier provides 100GB bandwidth and 1M edge requests/month, well beyond personal site needs.
- **Preview Deploys**: Automatic per-PR preview deployments via Vercel's GitHub integration.
- **Production Deploy**: Automatic on push/merge to main.
- **Domain**: Custom domain (matthew-field.ca) pointed to Vercel via DNS. Existing registrar unchanged.

## Technical Requirements & Constraints

### Performance
- Static pages should achieve 90+ Lighthouse performance score
- Minimize client-side JavaScript — server components by default. Note: Next.js ships ~60-85KB of baseline JS on every page (React runtime, client router, navigation components) regardless of content interactivity. This loads asynchronously and does not block initial paint. 90+ Lighthouse is achievable despite this baseline.
- Images optimized via Next.js Image component (automatic WebP/AVIF, lazy loading, responsive sizes)

### Compatibility
- **Browsers**: Last 2 versions of Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge. Mobile Safari and Chrome on iOS/Android.
- **Responsive**: Desktop, tablet, and mobile breakpoints. Mobile is a first-class target (recruiters viewing on phones).

### Accessibility
- WCAG 2.1 AA conformance target
- Semantic HTML, keyboard navigation, sufficient color contrast in both themes
- Radix UI primitives provide correct ARIA attributes for interactive components
- Alt text for all images

### Security
- **Contact form**: Server-side input validation via zod schema (field types, max lengths, email format). User-provided fields sent as plain text via Resend's `text` parameter (no HTML rendering of user input). Honeypot field (hidden input that bots fill but humans don't) for spam prevention — stops ~90% of naive bot submissions; does not stop targeted or headless-browser attacks, which is acceptable for a personal site's threat model. Per-IP rate limiting deferred to post-launch — Vercel serverless functions are stateless, so rate limiting requires an external state store (Vercel KV / Upstash Redis). Added reactively if spam exceeds acceptable threshold, monitored via Resend dashboard.
- **Email obfuscation**: react-obfuscate to deter scrapers.
- **CSP headers**: Route-scoped Content Security Policy configured via path-based headers in `next.config.js`. Content pages: `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'` (Next.js requires inline scripts for hydration — `'self'` alone breaks every page), `style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'`, `img-src 'self' data:`, `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'self'`, `frame-src 'self'`, restrictive `connect-src`. Playground routes (`/playground/*`): effectively opt out of CSP — permissive policy to allow inline styles, external resources, and dynamic code execution. This is acceptable because playground items have no auth, no stored data, and no sensitive operations.
- No user authentication, no stored user data beyond transient form submissions.

## Technical Decisions & Rationale

### Decision Log

1. **Next.js over Astro**: Astro would ship zero JavaScript on content pages, produce truly static output deployable to any CDN, and support strict `script-src 'self'` CSP without `'unsafe-inline'` (since Astro injects no inline scripts). Next.js was chosen for DX simplicity: a single dev server, single build, single deployment pipeline, and a unified React component model across content pages and interactive playground items. The tradeoffs are ~60-85KB of baseline JavaScript on every page, tighter coupling to Vercel for optimal deployment, and a weaker CSP (`'unsafe-inline'` required for hydration). This is accepted — the JS loads asynchronously without blocking paint, 90+ Lighthouse is achievable, the CSP still provides meaningful protection via other directives, and migration to another Next.js host is a weekend task, not a rewrite. Content (MDX files) is fully portable regardless of framework.

2. **MDX over plain markdown**: Low-cost optionality. MDX files without components behave identically to markdown. The cost is slightly slower compilation, no JSX rendering in standard markdown previewers, and React-style error messages for syntax errors. Keeps the door open for embedding interactive elements in blog posts or project writeups without a migration.

3. **Velite over rolling our own content loader**: Provides typed frontmatter schemas and build-time validation for ~15 minutes of setup. Catches broken content before it reaches production. Less code to maintain than a hand-rolled pipeline.

4. **Pagefind over Fuse.js**: Pagefind generates a compressed index at build time rather than requiring all content to be loaded into browser memory. Better performance for a growing blog.

5. **shadcn/ui over a traditional component library (MUI, Chakra)**: The component composition layer is owned source code, not an opaque dependency — full control over markup and styling to match any design direction without fighting a library's opinions. Radix UI primitives remain npm dependencies (typically 5-15 `@radix-ui/*` packages), but the dependency surface is smaller and more stable than a full component library, and Radix is actively maintained (Workos-backed).

6. **Vercel over Cloudflare Pages**: Vercel is zero-config for Next.js — no adapter layer, no edge runtime compatibility concerns. Cloudflare's unlimited bandwidth is appealing but unnecessary at personal site scale, and the OpenNext adapter introduces friction.

7. **Single package over monorepo**: The site is one Next.js app maintained by one person. Monorepo tooling adds overhead with no current benefit. Playground items needing dependency isolation use iframe embedding, not workspace extraction. Workspace extraction (pnpm workspaces) is a deliberate architectural decision reserved for cases where multiple playground items share a conflicting dependency tree — it is not a casual fallback, as it involves decoupling imports, setting up separate build config, and updating CI.

8. **Shiki over Prism**: Build-time highlighting with no client JS. Supports VS Code themes for familiar, high-quality syntax coloring.

## Known Limitations

- **Playground dependency conflicts**: The single-package structure means all playground items share one dependency tree. Items with conflicting dependencies use iframe isolation. This is expected to be rare.
- **Search scope**: Pagefind indexes static HTML output. Dynamically rendered playground content won't be searchable. This is acceptable — search is primarily for blog posts and written content.
- **Contact form delivery**: Relying on Resend means form submissions fail if the service is down. For a personal site, this risk is acceptable versus running custom email infrastructure.
- **Velite ecosystem longevity**: Velite is a relatively niche tool filling the same role as the abandoned Contentlayer. If Velite is abandoned, the migration path is replacing it with a hand-rolled pipeline using gray-matter + zod (~300-400 lines of utility code, plus import path updates across consuming files for the new collection types). Content files (MDX with frontmatter) would not need to change — only the build-time processing layer.
- **Next.js baseline JavaScript**: Every page ships ~60-85KB of JavaScript (React runtime + client router + navigation components) regardless of whether the page content is interactive. This is an architectural tradeoff of choosing Next.js over a zero-JS static generator. It does not block initial paint and does not prevent achieving 90+ Lighthouse scores. Hydration does affect TBT (Total Blocking Time) and INP (Interaction to Next Paint) — ~50ms on modern devices, 200-400ms on budget Android. The target audience (recruiters, tech professionals) is overwhelmingly on modern devices, so this is an acceptable tradeoff.
- **CSP limitations**: Next.js requires `'unsafe-inline'` for scripts due to inline hydration scripts injected on every page. A strict `script-src 'self'`-only policy is not achievable with Next.js static generation. The specified CSP still provides meaningful protection against resource injection (`object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'self'`, restrictive `connect-src`) but does not protect against inline script injection. Playground routes effectively opt out of CSP entirely.
- **Contact form rate limiting deferred**: Per-IP rate limiting requires an external state store (Vercel KV / Upstash Redis) because Vercel serverless functions are stateless. Deferred to post-launch to avoid an unplanned dependency. Honeypot provides baseline spam protection at launch; Resend usage monitored via their dashboard.
- **Turbopack/Webpack divergence**: CSS `@layer` ordering and CSS Modules class name hashing may differ between Turbopack (dev) and Webpack (production). Playground style isolation that works in dev could break in production. Mitigated by verifying playground items via Vercel preview deploys before merging.
